title: The divine messengers
hookLine: Yama asks: didn't you see the baby, the old, the sick, the dead?

cards: A smoke alarm chirps. Low battery. You think: I'll deal with it later.
It chirps again a week later, and again a week after that. Every chirp is a message, and none of them shouts.
The hundred and thirtieth discourse imagines a person after death, brought before Yama, the king of the dead in Indian tradition. Yama doesn't open with a list of crimes. He asks questions.
Good man, didn't you see the first messenger of the gods when it appeared among people? And the person says: no, sir, I didn't.

teach.h: A BABY, AN ELDER, SOMEONE SICK
teach.b: Then Yama explains. Didn't you ever see a tiny baby, lying helpless in its own mess? And didn't it occur to you: I too was born; let me do good while I can?
The second messenger: an old person, eighty, ninety, a hundred, bent like a roof beam, leaning on a stick, trembling. The third: someone sick, in pain, lifted and laid down by others.
The fourth: someone caught for a crime and punished. The fifth: a dead body, a day or two or three gone. Each time Yama asks the same thing: didn't it occur to you that you are subject to this too?
Then the line at the center.
This harm wasn't done by your mother or father, your brother or sister, your friends, your relatives, or the gods. You did it, and you will feel its fruit. It's stern.
But listen to who these messengers are. Not angels with trumpets. A baby.
A grandparent. A patient. A body.
They appear among ordinary people every day.
Many Buddhists hear an echo of the four sights that, in the traditional life story, moved young Siddhartha to leave the palace: an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering monk.
And the discourse ends with a surprise: Yama himself wishes he could be born human, hear a Buddha teach, and understand.
Even the judge of the dead wants the chance the living have.

how: Buddhists often reflect on aging, sickness and death as everyday reminders to practice, and the four sights of the young Siddhartha are retold at festivals and in temple murals across Buddhist countries.

o: a god who carries prayers up to heaven
an angel sent down to judge the dead
a divine messenger, like an elder or a baby

games.q: the five messengers: tap the pairs.
p: an old person, bent, with a stick
wishes he could be born human

s: in MN 130 there are five divine messengers
a baby, an old person, a sick person, a punished wrongdoer and a dead body.
Yama blames the person's parents for their wrongs
he says the harm wasn't done by parents, friends or gods: you did it.
the messengers in the discourse are angels sent from heaven
they are ordinary people met in daily life: the baby, the elder, the sick, the dead.

games.q: you're Yama, the judge of the dead. at the end of the discourse, what do you wish for?
o: to be born human, hear a Buddha and understand.
games.why: even the king of the dead longs for a human birth and the chance to hear the teaching.

practice: Bring to mind someone you saw recently, an infant in a stroller, an older neighbor on the stairs, a friend who's ill, and let them be a messenger, not of fear, but of a plain fact: I'm a body too, and this time is limited.
Let that make the next breath a little more awake, then rest.

wordCard.voice: Devaduta. Messenger of the gods: birth, aging, sickness, punishment and death, appearing among ordinary people, asking each of us, didn't you notice?

orig.note: Pali devaduta: messenger of the gods. the title of MN 130.

carryVoice: Your line: the messengers came. They come quietly, among ordinary people, every day. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 130, Devaduta Sutta (the divine messengers)
